reasoning_summary: The reduction (Hamiltonian Path instance H with n vertices -> G = H plus 17 isolated vertices, so |V(G)| = n+17 and the target path length is exactly n) is correct in both directions. Forward: a Hamiltonian path of H is a simple path of G on exactly n = |V(G)|-17 vertices. Backward: any simple path of G on n >= 2 vertices lies in one connected component and so cannot touch an isolated added vertex; hence it uses n distinct vertices of V_H = n vertices, i.e. it is a Hamiltonian path of H, and G's edges among V_H are exactly E_H. I tried to build counterexamples at the two risky spots and both failed to break the iff. (a) The sentence at lines 0032-0034 ('any set of n distinct vertices of G must include all of V_H') is literally false -- e.g. n = 3, V_H = {v1,v2,v3}, the 3-set {u1,u2,v1} omits v1's neighbours -- but it is superseded by the isolated-vertex argument on lines 0034-0042 and the final inference at lines 0045-0049 uses only that argument, so it is not load-bearing. (b) The degenerate case n = 1 (H a single vertex, G on 18 vertices) makes the parenthetical justification 'PG visits n > 1 vertices' inapplicable, since the path could be the single isolated vertex u1; but in that case H does have a (trivial) Hamiltonian path anyway, so the iff still holds, and NP-hardness only needs the reduction to be correct on the (infinitely many) instances with n >= 2. Construction is clearly polynomial time, and membership in NP is correctly noted. No counterexample to a claim the proof actually relies on.
